editorial_contributions.text:
Introduction: This paper is a survey presenting fast algorithms for several useful arithmetic operations on polynomials, power series, integers, real numbers, and 2-adic numbers. Each section focuses on one algorithm for one operation, and describes seven features of the algorithm:

Input: What numbers are provided to the algorithm? Sections 2, 3, 4, and
5 explain how various mathematical objects are represented as inputs.

Output: What numbers are computed by the algorithm?

Speed: How many coefficient operations does the algorithm use to perform a polynomial operation? The answer is at most \(n^{1+o(1)}\), where \(n\) is the problem size; each section states a more precise upper bound, often using the function defined in Section 4.

How it works: What is the algorithm? The algorithm may use previous
algorithms as subroutines.

The integer case (except in Section 2): The inputs were polynomials (or
power series); what about the analogous operations on integers (or real
numbers)? What difficulties arise in adapting the algorithm to integers?

How much time does the adapted algorithm take?

History: How were these ideas developed?

Improvements: The algorithm was chosen to be reasonably simple (subject to the \(n^{1+o(1)}\) bound) at the expense of speed; how can the same function be computed even more quickly?

Sections 2 through 5 describe fast multiplication algorithms for various rings. 2. Product: the FFT case. 3. Product: extension. 4. Product: zero-padding and localization. 5. Product: completion. 

The remaining sections describe various applications of fast multiplication. Here is a simplified summary of the functions being computed: 


6. Reciprocal. \(f\mapsto 1/f\) approximation. 


7. Quotient. \(f,h\mapsto h/f\) approximation. 


8. Logarithm. \(f\mapsto \log f\) approximation. 


9. Exponential. \(f\mapsto \exp f\) approximation (see also \S15 and \S16). 


10. Power. \(f,e\mapsto f^e\) approximation. 


11. Matrix product. \(f,g\mapsto fg\) for \(2\times 2\) matrices. 


12. Product tree. \(f_1,f_2,f_3,\dots\mapsto\) tree of products including \(f_1f_2f_3\cdots\). 


13. Sum of fractions. \(f_1,g_1,f_2,g_2,\dots\mapsto f_1/g_1+f_2/g_2+\cdots\). 


14. Fraction from continued fraction. \(q_1,q_2,\dots\mapsto q_1+1/(q_2+1/(\cdots))\). 


15. Exponential: the short case. 


16. Exponential: the general case. 


17. Quotient and remainder. \(f,h\mapsto \lfloor h/f\rfloor\), \(h\bmod f\). 


18. Remainder tree. \(h,f_1,f_2,\dots\mapsto h\bmod f_1,h\bmod f_2,\dots\). 


19. Small factors of a product. \(S,h_1,h_2,\dots\mapsto S(h_1h_2\cdots)\) where \(S\) is a set of primes and \(S(h)\) is the subset of \(S\) dividing \(h\). 


20. Small factors of a sequence. \(S,h_1,h_2,\dots\mapsto S(h_1),S(h_2),\dots\). 


21. Continued fraction from fraction. \(f_1,f_2,\dots\mapsto q_1,q_2,q_3,\cdots\) with \(f_1/f_2=q_1+1/(q_2+1/(q_3+1(\cdots)))\). 


22. Greatest common divisor. \(f_1,f_2\mapsto \gcd\{f_1,f_2\}\). 


23. Interpolator. \(f_1,g_1,f_2,g_2,\dots\mapsto h\) with \(h\equiv f_j\pmod{g_j}\). 


24. Coprime base. \(f_1,f_2,\dots\mapsto\) coprime set \(S\) with \(f_1,f_2,\dots\in\langle S\rangle\). 



The paper ends with a good list of more than a hundred references.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1154.11002].

title.title: Fast multiplication and its applications

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Let \(S\) be a finite set of positive integers. A ``coprime base for \(S\)'' means a set \(P\) of positive integers such that (1) each element of \(P\) is coprime to every other element of \(P\) and (2) each element of \(S\) is a product of powers of elements of \(P\). There is a natural coprime base for \(S\). This paper introduces an algorithm that computes the natural coprime base for \(S\) in essentially linear time. The best previous result was a quadratic-time algorithm of \textit{E. Bach}, \textit{J. Driscoll} and \textit{J. Shallit} [J. Algorithms 15, No. 2, 199--222 (1993; Zbl 0784.11058)]. This paper also shows how to factor \(S\) into elements of \(P\) in essentially linear time. The algorithms use solely multiplication, exact division, gcd, and equality testing, so they apply to any free commutative monoid with fast algorithms for those four operations; for example, given a finite set \(S\) of monic polynomials over a finite field, the algorithms factor \(S\) into coprimes in essentially linear time. These algorithms can be used as a substitute for prime factorization in many applications.

editorial_contributions.text:
In July 2002 appeared online the preprint ``Primes is in P'', by Manindra Agrawal, Neeraj Kayal, and Nitin Saxena which describes a deterministic polynomial time algorithm (henceforth referred to as ``AKS'') to determine the primality of an integer \(n\). The appearance of such an algorithm was totally unexpected and unleashed a feeding frenzy among the primality testing community, as they searched for improvements. The essence of AKS is succinctly described in the present paper as ``combinatorics in a cyclotomic extension of \({\mathbb Z}/(n)\)'' and the first improvements came mainly from fine-tuning the combinatorics, though also from sharpening bounds on quantities used the the algorithm. Many of these improvements were incorporated in the published version [\textit{M. Agrawal, N. Kayal} and \textit{N. Saxena}, Ann. Math. (2) 160, No. 2, 781--793 (2004; Zbl 1071.11070)]. The published algorithm has complexity \(\widetilde{O}(\log n^{7.5})\), whereas in the preprint the complexity is only proved to be \(\widetilde{O}(\log n^{12})\) where the notation \(\widetilde O(m)\) means \(O(m\) polynomial in \(\log m)\)). 

A fundamental advance was made by \textit{P. Berrizbeitia} [Math. Comput. 74, 2043--2059 (2005; Zbl 1071.11071)]. The preprint appeared in 2003, who showed that, for \(n\) such that \(n^2-1\) is divisible by a power of 2 close to \((\log n)^2\), one can do the combinatorics in a Kummer, rather than cyclotomic, extension of \({\mathbb Z}/(n)\), and the resulting algorithm is \(\widetilde{O}(\log n^{4})\). Berrizbeitia's ideas were taken up by \textit{Q. Cheng} [Primality Proving via One Round in ECPP and One Iteration in AKS, to appear in J. Cryptology, Preprint at \url{http://www.cs.ou.edu/~qchengpub.html}], Mihailescu and Avanzi (unpublished) and Bernstein in the present paper. Chen showed how to apply Berrizbeitia's algorithm when one has any prime divisor of \(n-1\) close to \((\log n)^2\). Bernstein extends the algorithm to the case that one has an arbitrary divisor \(e \approx (\log n)^2\) of \(n^d-1\), where \(d \in n^{o(1)}\). The existence of a suitable pair \((d,e)\) for any prime \(n\) is proved in the paper, as a consequence of a theorem of Odlyzko and Pomerance. The resulting algorithm runs in time \((\log n^{4+o(1)})\). The basic theorem is:

Let \(n,d\) and \(e\) be positive integers such that \(2^e-1 \geq n^{2d\lfloor\sqrt{e}\rfloor}\) and \(e\) divides \(n^d-1\). Let \(f\) be a monic polynomial in \({\mathbb Z}/(n)[y]\) of degree \(d\). Define \(R\) as the ring \({\mathbb Z}/(n)[y]/f\). Let \(r\) be an element of \(R\) such that \(r^{n^d-1} =1\) in \(R\), \(r^{(n^d-1)/q}-1\) is a unit in \(R\) for each prime \(q\) dividing \(e\), and \(r-1\) is a unit in \(R\). If \((x-1)^{n^d}=r^{(n^d-1)/e}x-1\) in the ring \(R[x]/(x^e-r)\) then \(n\) is a power of a prime.

In fact a slightly refined version of the theorem is proved. Careful estimates of constant factors are given, and issues relevant to implementation discussed. Also included is a section on the relation between the work of Mihailescu and Avanzi and the current paper. It is still problematic as to whether the algorithm is truly practical, and competitive with (hyper)elliptic curve algorithms or, indeed, the subexponential algorithm usually known as APRCL [see \textit{H. Cohen} and \textit{H. W. Lenstra, jun.}, Math. Comput. 42, 297--330 (1984; Zbl 0578.10004)] which in practice is extremely efficient. In this respect the author conjectures that, in his algorithm, \(d=1\) is the only relevant case, since if \(d>1\) one can follow Chen (loc. cit.) and use an elliptic curve step to replace \(n\) by an auxiliary \(n^\prime\) that-one hopes- has suitable divisors of \(n^\prime -1\). Conjecturally, the elliptic curve step takes time \(O((\log n)^{3+o(1)}\), so is worthwhile -- even if it has to be repeated several times in order to reduce to \(d=1\). Experiment seems to confirm this, but nothing is proved. Finally, it should be noted that all the AKS-type algorithms in the Berrizbeitia line introduce a random element. To the reviewer's knowledge, the only strictly deterministic polynomial time primality test is the original, cyclotomic version of AKS.

editorial_contributions.text: A perfect power is an integer \(n>1\) that can be written as \(n=x^k\) for integers \(x,k\) with \(k>1\). This paper presents an algorithm for computing approximate \(k\)th roots and determining if an integer \(n\) is a perfect power; the algorithm runs in \((\log n)^{1+o(1)}\) bit operations. The key idea is to compute approximate \(k\)th roots using only a minimal number of bits of precision in Newton's method. Specifying the many details correctly and proving the running time of this seemingly simple algorithm comprises the bulk of this rather lengthy, but well-written paper. Of independent interest is the adaptation of a theorem of Loxton on multiple linear forms in logarithms to bound the number of perfect powers in a short interval.

title.title: Faster addition and doubling on elliptic curves

editorial_contributions.text: Let \(p_i(t)\), \(1\leq i\leq 4\), be a polynomial with integral rational coefficients. The author develops a fast method of finding the solutions of the Diophantine equation \(\sum_{i=1}^4 p_i(x_i)= 0\), \(x\in \mathbb{Z}^4\), and applies his algorithm to exhibit the smallest integer representable as a sum of two cubes of (positive) integers in \(k\) different ways for \(k\leq 7\) \((k\leq 5)\), to list 516 solutions of the equation \(x_1^4+ x_2^4=x_3^4+ x_4^4\) (with h.c.f. \((x_1,x_2, x_3,x_4)= 1\)), to give the seven (essentially different) positive solutions with \(x_4\leq 2.1\cdot 10^7\) of the Euler equation \(x_1^4+ x_2^4+ x_3^4= x_4^4\), and to a few other problems.

title.title: Enumerating solutions to \(p(a)+q(b)=r(c)+s(d)\)

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: This paper reviews, from bottom to top, a polynomial-time algorithm to correct \(t\) errors in classical binary Goppa codes defined by squarefree degree-\(t\) polynomials. The proof is factored through a proof of a simple Reed-Solomon decoder, and the algorithm is simpler than Patterson's algorithm. All algorithm layers are expressed as Sage scripts backed by test scripts. All theorems are formally verified. The paper also covers the use of decoding inside the Classic McEliece cryptosystem, including reliable recognition of valid inputs.

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper surveys (and in some cases improves on) previous results on finding (a) divisors in residue classes, (b) divisors in short intervals, (c) modular roots, (d) high-power divisors, and (e) correcting ``codeword errors'' in arithmetical codes (i.e., elements of \(\text{GF}(p_1)\times \text{GF}(p_1)\times \dots \times \text{GF}(p_n)\), where \(p_1,\dots,p_n\) are distinct primes). It is very well-written and readable, with lots of examples. Since many of its results directly impact cryptographic techniques, this paper is of particular interest to those in computational number theory and cryptography.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1154.11002].

title.title: Hash-function based PRFs: AMAC and its multi-user security

editorial_contributions.text:
In the paper a construction of a variable-length input unpredictable random function from a fixed-length unpredictable random function is given. Particularly, so called ``protected counter sum'' construction is given and shown that if the underlying function is unpredictable then also the function resulting from the construction is unpredictable. 


While relevant ideas in the protected counter sum construction seem to be published previously, here the exact security analysis, albeit in a rather terse, ``telegraphic'' style is given. Also several advantages over known chaining and cascading techniques are briefly discussed.

title.title: Inverted Edwards coordinates

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(\Psi(H,y)\) denote the number of integers in \([1,H]\) with no prime factor exceeding \(y\). The author describes procedures for determining upper and lower bounds for \(\Psi\) that can be computed at very high speed. The level of accuracy depends on the choice of a parameter \(\alpha\), but quite close bounds can be found; this is illustrated by comparing the bounds obtained for \(\Psi(H,y)/H\) when \(H= 2^{300}\), \(y= 2^{30}\) with that for the well-known approximation \(\rho({\log H\over\log y})\) where \(\rho\) is the Dickman function.

 The author remarks that bounds of a similar type were obtained by \textit{D. Coppersmith} in [Math. Comput. 54, 895--902 (1990; Zbl 0701.11008)]. The improvements derived in the current paper emanate from the algebraic framework for one-variable discrete generalized power series described in section 2 in which the notions of a series over \(\mathbb{Q}\) and a distribution over \(\mathbb{Q}\) are investigated, and the fast algorithm presented in section 3. In section 4, the author discusses the accuracy of his approximations and the choice of the parameter \(\alpha\), whilst generalizations of the problem are described in section 5. The reader will appreciate the extensive list of references at the end of the paper.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1002.00005].

editorial_contributions.text: Given power series \(u, v\) with first \(n\) terms and with \(v(0)=0\), over a finite commutative ring \(R\), the paper gives an algorithm for computation of the first \(n\) terms of \(u(v)\), when \(R\) has a non-zero characteristic. This is done in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) ring operations; this is fast, when \(R\) has a small characteristic. The procedure is discussed for prime and prime power characteristic, then the chinese remainder theorem is invoked for other cases (Knuth).

title.title: The tangent FFT

editorial_contributions.text:
Traditionally any computation on elliptic curves was done using the Weierstrass normal form. Edwards introduced a new normal form for elliptic curves based on an embedding of the curve in \(\mathbb{P}^1 \times \mathbb{P}^1\). Edwards models were the first curves shown to have a complete addition law, i.e., the addition formulas work for all pairs of input with no exception for neutral element, negatives etc. But even complete Edwards curves can become incomplete after a suitable quadratic extension.

The authors in this paper give a complete set of addition laws for the Edwards curve 
\[
 \bar{E}_{E,a,d}=\{ \big( (X:Z),(Y,T) \big) \in \mathbb{P}^1 \times \mathbb{P}^1: aX^2T^2+Y^2Z^2=Z^2T^2+dX^2Y^2 \}, 
\]
 where \(a,d\) are distinct non zero elements of a field \(k\) with characteristic \(\mathrm{char}(k)\neq 2\).

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(f\) be a nonconstant squarefree polynomial of \(\mathbb{Z}[X]\) and \(c,H,h\in\mathbb{Z}\) with \(H>0\) and \(h>2\log H\). The paper under review presents an algorithm for the following problem: Which of the values \(f(c+1)\), \(f(c+2),\dots,f(c+H)\) are locally square at all primes \(p\geq h\) (i.e., square in the \(p\)-adic field \(\mathbb{Q}_p)\). It is proved that the average time for this algorithm, when \(c\) is a uniform random element of an interval of length about \(H^2\), is \(H/M^{2+o(1)}\), where \(M=H^{1/\text{lglog}H}\), for fixed \(f\) as \(H\to\infty\), provided that \(c\) has at most \(M^{o(1)}\) digits and \(h\) is in \(M^{o(1)}\). Moreover, the paper presents the results of two record-setting computations: an enumeration of locally square integers up to \(24\times 2^{64}\) and an enumeration of all small coprime integer pairs \((x,y)\) such that \(x^3+y^7\) is locally square at all primes \(p<300\).

title.title: Never trust a bunny

editorial_contributions.text:
The authors study the elliptic-curve single-scalar multiplication over finite fields, i.e. given a finite field \(k\) (the ground field), an elliptic curve \(E\) (with small parameters), an integer \(n\) (the scalar) and a point \(P\in E(k)\), they identify today's fastest methods to compute the point \(nP\) on \(E\). Due to the well-known cryptographic applications, tables and figures are given for \(160\), \(256\) and \(512\)-bit scalars, expressing the necessary number of multiplications per bit as a function of the \textbf{I}/\textbf{M} ratio, i.e. the number of multiplications needed to provide an inversion in the ground field.

In order to do this, the authors first consider the problem of adding two points (or doubling a point). They look at twelve different coordinate systems: Projective, Jacobian (these two systems are also considered in the particular, faster, case \(a_4=-3\)), Doubling (\textit{resp.} Tripling)-oriented Doche/Icart/Kohel, Montgomery, Jacobi intersections, Jacobi quartics, Hessian, Edwards and inverted Edwards. For each system, the relation with the classical Weierstrass model and the corresponding (affine) coordinates is given. Note that certain systems do not provide a model for every elliptic curve.

Since the precomputation of some little multiples \(2P,3P,5P,7P,\cdots,mP\) is necessary, they look for the optimal odd \(m\) (always less than \(31\)), constructing for each \(m,n\) an ``addition-subtraction'' chain, that allows a fast computation of \(nP\). In order to do this, they combine ``windows'' techniques, and average over many random scalars of given size to get the best choice.

Finally, the authors consider four cases, allowing zero, one, two or three inversions in the ground field (typically, an inversion is needed when one wants to give the affine coordinates of a point). Then they compare their respective performances when the ratio \textbf{I}/\textbf{M} varies.

All the results are summarized in three tables, and the fastest ones in three figures, giving a clear account of what is known about this problem nowadays. Note also that all these results are updated at the address \url{http://hyperelliptic.org/EFD}.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1141.11002].

editorial_contributions.text:
The \(3x+1\) map \(T\) is defined by \(T(x)=(3x+1)/2\) for \(x\) odd, \(T(x)=x/2\) for \(x\) even. On the ring \(\mathbb Z_2\) of 2-adic integers, the 2-adic shift map \(S:\mathbb Z_2\to\mathbb Z_2\) is defined by \(S(x)=(x-1)/2\) if \(x\equiv 1\bmod 2\), \(S(x)=x/2\) if \(x\equiv 0\bmod 2\). Now the \(3x+1\) conjugacy map \(\Phi\) is uniquely determined by \(\Phi\circ S\circ\Phi^{-1}=T\) and \(\Phi(0)=0\). The function \(\Phi\) is shown to be solenoidal, i.e., it induces permutations \(\Phi_n\) on \(\mathbb Z/2^n\mathbb Z\). Moreover, \(\Phi_n\) takes odd numbers to odd numbers, whence it induces a permutation \(\hat\Phi_n\) on \(({\mathbb Z}/2^n{\mathbb Z})^*\). In terms of \(\Phi\), the well-known \(3x+1\) conjecture is reformulated to \({\mathbb Z}^+\subseteq\Phi({1\over 3}{\mathbb Z})\), where \(\mathbb Z^+\) denotes the positive integers. The following Periodicity Conjecture: \(\Phi({\mathbb Q}\cap{\mathbb Z}_2)={\mathbb Q}\cap{\mathbb Z}_2\), if true, would imply that iteration of \(T\) cannot produce a divergent trajectory.


The main subject of this paper is to study the cycle structure of the \(\hat\Phi_n\), which, in turn, determines the cycle structure of the \(\Phi_n\). The cycle of \(\Phi_n\) containing \(x\) is denoted by \(\sigma_n(x)\). Call a cycle \(\sigma_n(x)\) of \(\Phi_n\) inert if it lifts to a single cycle \(\sigma_{n+1}(x)\) of \(\Phi_{n+1}\); \(\sigma_n(x)\) is called stable if \(\sigma_m(x)\) is inert for any \(m\geq n\). Main theorem on \(\Phi\): Suppose that \(|\sigma_n(x)|\geq4\) and that \(\sigma_n(x)\) and \(\sigma_{n+1}(x)\) are both inert. Then \(\sigma_{n+2}(x)\) is also inert. There is also a generalization to \(ax+b\) conjugacy maps. In addition, empirical material and heuristic arguments concerning the cycle structure of \(\hat\Phi_n\) are given. The empirical data suggest the Fixed Point Conjecture: \(\Phi\) has exactly two odd fixed points, and the \(3x+1\) Conjugacy Finiteness Conjecture: For each \(j\geq0\), \(\Phi\) has finitely many odd periodic points of period \(2^j\). Two appendices concerning solenoidal maps close the paper.

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: Pollard's rho algorithm, along with parallelized, vectorized, and negating variants, is the standard method to compute discrete logarithms in generic prime-order groups. This paper presents two reasons that Pollard's rho algorithm is farther from optimality than generally believed. First, ``higher-degree local anticollisions'' make the rho walk less random than the predictions made by the conventional Brent-Pollard heuristic. Second, even a truly random walk is suboptimal, because it suffers from ``global anticollisions'' that can at least partially be avoided. For example, after \((1.5+o(1))\sqrt{\ell}\) additions in a group of order \(\ell\) (without fast negation), the baby-step-giant-step method has probability \(0.5625+o(1)\) of finding a uniform random discrete logarithm; a truly random walk would have probability \(0.6753\ldots +o(1)\); and this paper's new two-grumpy-giants-and-a-baby method has probability \(0.71875+o(1)\).

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1295.11003].

editorial_contributions.text:
The still open ``\(3x+1\)''-problem (or ``Collatz''- or ``Hasse''- or ``Syracuse''- or ``Kakutani''-problem) is to prove that for every \(n\in \mathbb{N}\) there exists a \(k\) with \(T^{(k)} (n)=1\) where the function \(T(n)\) takes odd numbers \(n\) to \((3n+1 )/2\) and even numbers \(n\) to \(n/2\). In this note under review the author gives an equivalent statement using 2-adic integers \(\mathbb{Z}_ 2\): Let \(Q\in \mathbb{Z}_ 2\) with \(Q= 2^{d_ 0}+ 2^{d_ 1}+ \cdots\), where \(0\leq d_ 0 <d_ 1< \cdots\) then the permutation \(\Phi\) of \(\mathbb{Z}_ 2\) is defined by \(\Phi(Q)= (- {1\over 3}) 2^{d_ 0}+ (- {1\over 9}) 2^{d_ 1}+ \cdots\).


Then it is proved that the ``\(3x+1\)''-conjecture is equivalent to the conjecture that \(3Q\) is an integer if \(\Phi(Q)\) is a positive integer. It turns out that this map \(\Phi\) is just the inverse of a well studied function \(Q_ \infty\) [see \textit{J. C. Lagarias}, Am. Math. Mon. 92, 3-23 (1985; Zbl 0566.10007)]. New is the explicit formula for \(\Phi= Q_ \infty^{-1}\).


Finally the author gives some applications of his definition, including a proof that the function \(\Phi\) is in \(\mathbb{Z}_ 2\) nowhere differentiable, a result which was proved earlier by the reviewer [see Mitt. Math. Ges. Hamb. 12, 231-251 (1991; Zbl 0773.11018)].

title.title: Computing small discrete logarithms faster

editorial_contributions.text:
The problem of listing all the prime numbers up to a fixed bound \(N\) is very old going back, at least, to the classic sieve of Eratostenes.

\textit{P. Pritchard} [J. Algorithms 4, 332--344 (1983; Zbl 0546.10004)] posed the question of the existence of an algorithm able to find such a listing using \(o(N)\) operations (loads, stores, comparisons, additions and subtractions of \(O(\log N))\) - bits integers) and \(O(N^{\alpha})\) bits of memory for some \(\alpha < 1\). The present paper gives an affirmative answer to this question. The tool used is the enumeration of the values taken by certain integral binary quadratic forms.

 As the authors point out, in the language of quadratic forms, the sieve of Eratosthenes can be interpreted as the enumeration of the natural numbers represented by the reducible quadratic form \(xy\). They consider instead some irreducible binary quadratic forms.

More concretely they consider the three following quadratic forms: \(4x^2+y^2\) for the primes \(p\equiv 1 \bmod 4\), \(3x^2+y^2\) for the primes \(p\equiv 7 \bmod 12\)\, and \(3x^2+y^2\) for the primes \(p\equiv 11 \bmod 12\)\, (as the authors point out many other choices are possible). The algorithm uses the propriety that, in the three cases, a natural number \(n\) is prime if and only if the number of positive representations \((x,y)\) of \(n\) (and \(x>y>0\) in the third case) is odd.

The resulting algorithm uses \(O(N/\log\log N)\) operations and \(N^{1/2+o(1)}\) bits of memory. The authors also point out a later improvement of W. F. Galway that needs only \(N^{1/3+o(1)}\) bits of memory.

editorial_contributions.text:
An integer is \(y\)-smooth if it is not divisible by any primes larger than \(y\). Define \(\Psi(x,y)= \#\{n:1\leq n\leq x\) and \(n\) is \(y\)-smooth\}. This function \(\Psi\) is used to estimate the speed of various factoring methods. Section 4 presents a fast algorithm to compute arbitrarily tight upper and lower bounds on \(\Psi(x,y)\). For example, \(1.16\cdot 10^{45} <\Psi(10^{54},10^6)< 1.19\cdot 10^{45}\).


The idea of the algorithm is to bound the relevant Dirichlet series between two power series. Thus bounds are obtained on \(\Psi(x,y)\) for all \(x\) at one fell swoop. More general functions can be computed in the same way.

title.title: Twisted Edwards curves

editorial_contributions.text:
The author proposes a new, compact and highly readable representation for ideals of any order in a number field. The idea is the following. Any nonzero ideal contains some positive integer \(N\). Represent the ideal locally at all primes of \(\mathbb{Z}\) dividing \(N\). To avoid factorization problems in practice, instead of the set of prime divisors of \(N\) a coprime base \(P\) for \(N\) is used that is a pairwise coprime set of positive integers generating a semigroup that contains \(N\). This representation is compatible with ideal arithmetic: all usual ideal operations are local. It turns out that this representation is generally faster than the usual representations in the \(\mathbb{Z}\) basis or the two-element representation. The paper details the algorithms for this representation and for the basic operations.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0852.00023].

title.title: A low-resource quantum factoring algorithm

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: Let \(\mathcal{E}= \mathbb{F}_q\) be an elliptic curve, and \(P\) a point in \(\mathcal{E}(\mathbb{F}_q)\) of prime order \(\ell\). Vélu's formulæ let us compute a quotient curve \(\mathcal{E}' = \mathcal{E}\langle P\rangle\) and rational maps defining a quotient isogeny \(\phi:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{E}'\) in \(\widetilde{O}(\ell)\) \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-operations, where the \(\widetilde{O}\) is uniform in \(q\). This article shows how to compute \(\mathcal{E}'\), and \(\phi(Q)\) for \(Q\) in \(\mathcal{E}(\mathbb{F}_q)\), using only \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\ell})\) \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-operations, where the \(\widetilde{O}\) is again uniform in \(q\). As an application, this article speeds up some computations used in the isogeny-based cryptosystems CSIDH and CSURF.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1452.11005].

title.title: Hyper-and-elliptic-curve cryptography

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Fix pairwise coprime positive integers \(p_1,p_2,\dots,p_s\). We propose representing integers \( u\) modulo \( m\), where \( m\) is any positive integer up to roughly \(\sqrt{p_1p_2\cdots p_s}\), as vectors \((u\bmod p_1,u\bmod p_2,\dots,u\bmod p_s)\). We use this representation to obtain a new result on the parallel complexity of modular exponentiation: there is an algorithm for the common CRCW PRAM that, given positive integers \(x\), \(e\), and \(m\) in binary, of total bit length \(n\), computes \(x^e\bmod m\) in time \(O(n/{\lg\lg n})\) using \(n^{O(1)}\) processors. For comparison, a parallelization of the standard binary algorithm takes superlinear time; Adleman and Kompella gave an \(O((\lg n)^3)\) expected time algorithm using \(\exp(O(\sqrt{n\lg n}))\) processors; von zur Gathen gave an NC algorithm for the highly special case that \(m\) is polynomially smooth.

editorial_contributions.text:
In 1987, Hendrik W. Lenstra jun. introduced one of the best general integer factorization methods, the Elliptic-Curve Method (ECM). The state-of-the-art implementation is GMP-ECM, described in [\textit{P. Zimmermann} and \textit{B. Dodson}, ANTS-VII, Lect. Notes Comput. Sci. 4076, 525--542 (2006; Zbl 1143.11358)]. In this paper, a new ECM implementation is proposed, ``EECM-MPFQ'', and its background and speed results are presented.

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic \(> 2\) and \(a, d \in K\setminus \{0\}\) with \(a \neq d\). Recall that the twisted Edwards curve \(E_{E,a,d}\) is defined by the equation \(ax^2 + y^2 = 1 + dx^2y^2\). An Edwards curve is a twisted Edwards curve in which \(a = 1\).

The paper analyzes the impact of Edwards curves on ECM. Section 2 revises the group law on Edwards curves and twisted Edwards curves, and various coordinate systems for Edwards curves. Section 3 discuss points of small order on Edwards curves. Sections 4 and 5 are devoted to the use of Edwards curves inside ECM. In Section 6, the construction of Edwards curves having torsion group \(\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z\) or \(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z\) over \(\mathbb Q\) is explained. Further, it is proved that twisted Edwards curves cannot have torsion group \(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\times \mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z\) or \(Z/10Z\) over \(\mathbb Q\) and that twisted Edwards curves with torsion group \(\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z\) or \(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z\) over \(\mathbb Q\) cannot have curve parameter \(a = -1\). Section 7, describes the construction of infinite families of Edwards curves having torsion group \(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z\) and \(\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z\), adapting constructions of Atkin and Morain, and Montgomery, respectively, to the Edwards context. Section 8 describes how to find better choices of Edwards curves to use in EECM-MPFQ, i.e. twisted Edwards curves that simultaneously have small parameters \(a\) and \(d\), a small height nontorsion point and large torsion over \(Q\). Section 9 presents measurements of ECM success probabilities, demonstrating the necessity of choosing curves of a large torsion group. Finally, section 10 reports the overall effectiveness of EECM-MPFQ when parameters are chosen sensibly.

title.title: On the correct use of the negation map in the Pollard rho method

editorial_contributions.text:
From the abstract: ``The best attacks known against the McEliece cryptosystem have cost growing exponentially with the number of errors corrected by the error-correcting code used in the cryptosystem. One can modify the cryptosystem to asymptotically increase this number of errors, for the same key size and the same ciphertext size, by generalizing classical binary Goppa codes to subfield subcodes of algebraic-geometry codes, and then moving from genus 0 to higher genus. This paper introduces streamlined algorithms for code generation and decoding for a broad class of these codes; shows that this class includes classical binary Goppa codes; and shows that moving to higher genus within this class decodes more errors than classical binary Goppa codes for concrete sizes of cryptographic interest. A notable feature of this paper's algorithms is the use of arithmetic on the Jacobian variety of the underlying curve.''

The paper is built up as follows: The background, purpose, and contents of the paper is described in a thorough and detailed way in Section 1 (Introduction). In Section 2, the authors describe algebraic curves, the Riemann-Roch theorem, and AG codes. In particular they describe \(C_{a,b}\) curves, which play a main role in the article. In Section 3, they describe the family of codes studied in the paper. They include AG codes, and subfield subcodes of AG codes, and classical binary Goppa codes. In Sections 4 and 5, the authors describe a code-construction algorithm, and a corresponding decoding algorithm, respectively. In Section 6, they describe a McEliece public-key encryption scheme (PKE) based on codes described in the previous sections, as an alternative to a PKE built on classical Goppa codes. In Section 7, they give concrete examples in cases where the genus of the algebraic curves appearing is \(1\) (elliptic curves). The authors show that even this small change of genus gives concrete improvements compared to the usage of classical binary Goppa codes (where the curves are rational).

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1584.94002].

title.title: Starfish on strike

editorial_contributions.text:
The paper provides an algorithm that, given an integer \(n\), finds the largest integer \(k\) such that \(n\) is a \(kth\) power. The algorithm has run-time \(\log(n)(\log\log(n))^{O(1)}\), improving a previous algorithm by the first author [Math. Comput. 67, 1253--1283 (1998; Zbl 0910.11057)], taking time \(\log(n)^{1+o(1)}\).

The paper begins listing the three steps of the proposed algorithm: roughly the first step takes for each prime power \(q\) an approximation \(r_q\) to \(n^{1/q}\) while the second finds a 
factor base \(P\) of coprime integers such that \(n\) and each \(r_q\) are a product of powers of elements of \(P\). Finally step 3 finds \(k\) as a gcd.

Then the paper discuss details of the three steps, showing standard ways to perform each step in the mentioned time. Next the authors discuss the performance of the algorithm and they compare it with the previous algorithm of D. J. Bernstein. They point out that for almost all values of \(n\) the first step of the algorithm already reveals that \(k=1\).

Finally the authors review the history of the problem.

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: In this paper we consider the decremental single-source shortest paths (SSSP) problem, where given a graph \(G\) and a source node \(s\) the goal is to maintain shortest paths between \(s\) and all other nodes in \(G\) under a sequence of online adversarial edge deletions.

 In their seminal work, \textit{S. Even} and \textit{Y. Shiloach} [J. Assoc. Comput. Mach. 28, 1--4 (1981; Zbl 0454.68075)] presented an exact solution to the problem with only \(O(mn)\) total update time over all edge deletions. Their classic algorithm was the best known result for the decremental SSSP problem for three decades, even when approximate shortest paths are allowed.

 The first improvement over the Even-Shiloach algorithm was given by the first author and \textit{L. Roditty} [in: Proceedings of the 22nd annual ACM-SIAM symposium on discrete algorithms, SODA 2011. Philadelphia, PA: Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (SIAM); New York, NY: Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) 1355--1365 (2011; Zbl 1376.68061)], who for the case of an unweighted and undirected graph presented an approximate \((1+\epsilon)\) algorithm with constant query time and a total update time of \(O(n^{2+O(1/\sqrt{\log n})})\). This work triggered a series of new results, culminating in a recent breakthrough of \textit{M. Henzinger} et al. [``Decremental single-source shortest paths on undirected graphs in near-linear total update time'', in: Proceedings of the 2014 IEEE 55th annual symposium on foundations of computer science, FOCS '14. Washington, DC: IEEE Computer Society. 146--155 (2014)], who presented a \(\epsilon\)-approximate algorithm whose total update time is near linear \(O(m^{1+ O(1/\sqrt{\log n})})\). In this paper they posed as a major open problem the question of derandomizing their result.

 In fact, all known improvements over the Even-Shiloach algorithm are randomized. All these algorithms maintain some truncated shortest path trees from a small subset of nodes. While in the randomized setting it is possible to ``hide'' these nodes from the adversary, in the deterministic setting this is impossible: the adversary can delete all edges touching these nodes, thus forcing the algorithm to choose a new set of nodes and incur a new computation of shortest paths.

 In this paper we present the first deterministic decremental SSSP algorithm that breaks the Even-Shiloach bound of \(O(mn)\) total update time, for unweighted and undirected graphs. Our algorithm is \((1 + \epsilon)\) approximate and achieves a total update time of \(\tilde{O}(n^{2})\). Our algorithm can also achieve the same bounds in the incremental setting. It is worth mentioning that for dense instances where \(m = \Omega(n^{2-1/\sqrt{\log n}})\), our algorithm is also faster than all existing randomized algorithms.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1344.68018].

This positively answers a question posed in earlier work. Determining tight upper and lower bounds remains an open problem.

In these fields we need to be able to model complex shapes. Indeed, the method was originally proposed by P. Bezier and was used to model surfaces in automobile design. title.title: The use of Bernstein polynomials in CAD/CAM. Bezier curves

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We explain that in the study of the asymptotic expansion at the origin of a period-integral or of a hermitian period the computation of the Bernstein polynomial of the ``fresco'' (filtered differential equation) associated to the pair of germs of a holomorphic function with a holomorphic volume form gives a better control than the computation of the Bernstein polynomial of the full Brieskorn module of the germ of \(f\) at the origin. Moreover, it is easier to compute as it has a better functoriality and smaller degree. We illustrate this in the case where the polynomial \(f\) in \((n+1)\) variables has \((n+2)\) monomials and is not quasi-homogeneous, by giving an explicit simple algorithm to produce a multiple of this Bernstein polynomial in the case of a monomial holomorphic volume form. Several concrete examples are given.

editorial_contributions.text:
This work exposes a common framework for solving a series of problems from measure theory, harmonic analysis and probability theory in which certain functionals are to be represented by contents or measures of a wanted type, namely: the integral and Daniel's representation problems, moment problems of various kinds, several approximation problems of Bernstein type, the marginal problem, and the weak convergence and continuity problems.

After an introductory Chapter A where all these problems are defined, Chapter 1 is devoted to function spaces, while functionals and integrals are dealt with in Chapter 2. These two chapters lay the background for the integral representations discussed in the last Chapter 3. A bibliography of 19 items and an alphabetic index are appended.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1004.00019].

editorial_contributions.text: Let \(f\) be a holomorphic function with an isolated singularity at the origin relative to the corresponding eigenvalue \(\exp(2i\pi\alpha)\) of the monodromy. Assume that the \(p\)-th Bernstein polynomial (see [the author, ``Generalized Brieskorn modules. I: Convergent (a,b)-modules'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:2307.04395}]) of the \((a, b)\)-module generated by a germ of a holomorphic volume form \(\omega \in \Omega^{n+1}_0\) in the (convergent) Brieskorn \((a, b)\)-module associated to \(f\), has a root \(-\alpha - \mathbb N\). The author proves that there exists a pole of order at least \(p\) for the meromorphic extension of an analytic functional associated to \(\omega\) at some point in \(-\alpha - \mathbb N\). Among other things this implies the existence of at least \(p\) roots in \(-\alpha - \mathbb N\) (counting multiplicities) for the usual reduced Bernstein polynomial \(b_{f,0}\) of the germ of \(f\) at \(0\). The proof is based on the general theory of frescos developed in [the author, Boll. Unione Mat. Ital. (9) 2, No. 3, 651--697 (2009; Zbl 1193.32017)] and extended to the convergent case. It should be also noted that the main result is illustrated by a series of interesting examples where the higher Bernstein polynomials are calculated explicitly [the author, J. Singul. 25, 54--77 (2022; Zbl 1523.32049)].
